title: Meta ships Muse — its personal AI agent — to US users at $20 and $100 tiers
subtitle: The Hatch platform arrived under the production name Muse on September 8, priced far below the $199.99 rumor and running each task inside a visible browser in a dedicated cloud VM.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta launched Muse — the consumer AI agent previously reported as Project Hatch — on September 8, 2026, initially to US users only. The product ships with a free tier reported by Mark Zuckerberg at up to 100 million tokens per week, plus paid tiers of Power at $20 per month and Maximum at $100 per month. That is roughly ten times below the $199.99 sticker rumored in pre-launch reporting and puts Muse squarely on par with ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro rather than above them. Each Muse task runs inside a dedicated secure virtual machine in Meta's cloud, with a visible browser window the user can watch — deliberately not a hidden-agent product.

The connector list is the tell: Muse ships wired to Google Workspace, Ticketmaster, OpenTable, Spotify, and Apple Health, with checkout through Stripe's Link. Meta is choosing execution surfaces — booking, buying, scheduling — over pure information retrieval, and it is choosing Stripe as the payment rail rather than trying to route through Meta Pay. Distribution is the other half of the story: Muse reaches users through a standalone app, the web, and WhatsApp, with Meta's smart glasses on the roadmap. The company reaches roughly two billion daily users across Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, which is the largest built-in audience a consumer agent has ever launched into.

The frame Meta is using is Zuckerberg's phrase "personal superintelligence" — an AI that acts as a tireless assistant across every domain of the user's life. In practice the launch is Meta staking out consumer agents as its answer to OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude for Consumers, both of which have spent 2026 pushing hard on transactional workflows. Muse's showable-VM design is a direct response to the trust problem those competitors have run into: an agent that spends the user's money without a visible chain of what it did is a support-and-refund nightmare, and Meta appears to have designed around that failure mode from the start.

Takeaway for learners: consumer AI agents are becoming a distribution game, not a capability game. The reasoning quality of Muse, ChatGPT's agent mode, and Anthropic's computer-use offerings is now close enough that the winner will be decided by which app is already on the phone. If you are building for this layer, the interesting engineering is not the model — it is the connectors, the refund flow when the agent gets it wrong, and the transparency UI that convinces a user their agent did not just quietly buy the wrong thing. Watch the first-week complaint volume; that is the real benchmark.
